title: WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide
container: World Health Organization, Geneva (ISBN 9789240034228 electronic; 9789240034211 print)
supports: Table 0.1 of the guideline document itself gives the 2021 AQG levels as PM2.5 5 ug/m3 (annual) and 15 ug/m3 (24-hour); PM10 15 ug/m3 (annual) and 45 ug/m3 (24-hour); 24-hour values are the 99th percentile (i.e. 3-4 exceedance days per year).
note: Verified by reading the PDF text (IRIS bitstream) and the WHO publication page (date 22 Sep 2021, ISBN 9789240034228). Interim target 3 for 24-h PM2.5 is 37.5 ug/m3 (relevant to Thailand's 2023 standard). No DOI.

title: Global estimates of mortality associated with long-term exposure to outdoor fine particulate matter
container: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
supports: The Global Exposure Mortality Model (GEMM), built from 41 cohorts in 16 countries, predicts 8.9 million (95% CI 7.5-10.3) deaths in 2015 attributable to outdoor PM2.5, 120% larger than the risk function used in the GBD (4.0 million; 95% CI 3.3-4.8).
note: Crossref + abstract match. Full author list not captured here (check Crossref JSON in cr/).

title: The contribution of outdoor air pollution sources to premature mortality on a global scale
supports: Using a global atmospheric chemistry model, outdoor air pollution (mostly PM2.5) is calculated to lead to 3.3 (95% CI 1.61-4.81) million premature deaths per year worldwide, predominantly in Asia.
note: Crossref + Europe PMC abstract match.

title: Estimated global mortality attributable to smoke from landscape fires
supports: Principal estimate of average mortality attributable to landscape-fire-smoke exposure was 339,000 deaths annually (interquartile range of sensitivity analyses 260,000-600,000), with Southeast Asia (110,000) among the most affected regions; estimated annual mortality was 262,000 during La Nina versus 532,000 during El Nino.
note: Crossref abstract read directly; author list beyond first 5 should be confirmed from Crossref JSON cr/10.1289_ehp.1104422.json.

title: Public health impacts of the severe haze in Equatorial Asia in September-October 2015: demonstration of a new framework for informing fire management strategies to reduce downwind smoke exposure
supports: The authors estimate that haze in 2015 resulted in 100 300 excess deaths across Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, more than double those of the 2006 event, with much of the increase due to fires in Indonesia's South Sumatra Province.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract match; full author order to be confirmed against cr JSON before typesetting.

title: The 1997 haze disaster in Indonesia: its air quality and health effects
supports: After interviewing 543 people and conducting lung-function tests, more than 90% of respondents had respiratory symptoms, and PM10 and CO reached 'very unhealthy' and 'hazardous' PSI levels during the 1997 Indonesia haze.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Author list beyond first 5 (Yamamura...) to confirm in cr JSON.

title: Development and application of a United States-wide correction for PM2.5 data collected with the PurpleAir sensor
supports: Raw PurpleAir data overestimate PM2.5 concentrations by about 40% in most parts of the US under typical ambient and smoke-impacted conditions, and a linear regression with a relative-humidity term reduces much of this bias.
note: Abstract read from Crossref (truncated after 'adding a relative humidity t'); sentence taken from the first portion. Remaining details (RMSE) not captured.

supports: Using 2014-2017 northern Thailand outpatient data, same-day PM10 was associated with chronic lower respiratory disease visits (IRR 1.020, 95% CI 1.012-1.028) and cerebrovascular disease visits (IRR 1.020, 95% CI 1.004-1.035), with no association for ischaemic heart disease (IRR 0.994, 95% CI 0.974-1.014); PM10 peaked in March, coinciding with peak biomass burning.
note: Crossref/OpenAlex abstract; study area is northern Thailand (not only Chiang Mai).

supports: In Upper Northern Thailand all-cause mortality risk increased by 0.9% (95% CI 0.1-1.8) per 10 ug/m3 increase in same-day vegetation-fire PM2.5 and by 12.8% (95% CI 10.5-15.1) on extreme-heat (90th percentile) days, with no interactive effect.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: In upper northern Thailand 2013-2022, during haze periods COPD fatality and re-admission rates rose significantly (mean difference 0.43 and 4.23 per 1000 cases, p<0.001) while lung cancer fatality was higher without statistical significance; PM2.5 exceeded air quality standards from January to April.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: CMAQ-ISAM simulations for 2019 show open biomass burning substantially impacts PM2.5 in Thailand's Upper Northern Region, with Myanmar the major contributor in the west and central sub-regions and domestic burning the major contributor in the east during peak months; transboundary transport from Myanmar also raised Bangkok PM2.5 in March-April.
note: No percentage numbers are given in the abstract; read the full text for contribution figures before quoting numbers.

supports: WRF-HYSPLIT analysis found Burma accounted for 37% of all Southeast Asian hotspot locations in March, and monsoon flow can bring pollutants from Burma and Laos toward northern Thailand in March, likely contributing to high PM2.5 there.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: Radiocarbon and organic-marker source apportionment at Chiang Mai sites in 2018 found biomass-burning-derived OC was 65.5 +/- 5.8% (urban) and 79.9 +/- 7.6% (rural) of total carbon in the high burning season versus 39.1 +/- 7.9% and 42.8 +/- 4.6% in the low season.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: Fire aerosols were responsible for nearly all very-low-visibility (<7 km) events in Southeast Asia and up to 39% of low-visibility (<10 km) events in Bangkok; mainland Southeast Asian burning accounts for 99% of fire-produced PM2.5 in Bangkok.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Also useful for the visibility-PM link (D17) and as a transboundary-character citation.

supports: The authors argue that administrative fragmentation and the protection of vested economic interests by Thai business and political elites have compromised transboundary governance of the air in Thailand, and recommend legislation centred on cross-sectoral and cross-jurisdictional cooperation.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Author listed as Marks, Danny and Miller, Michelle Ann (confirm in cr JSON).

supports: Species-tagged modelling attributes about 900 thousand premature deaths per year in Southeast Asia to air pollution, 77% from local emissions and 23% from transboundary air pollution, with TAP impacts especially adverse in border regions and in Laos.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Regional (not mainland/northern Thailand-specific).

supports: The overview summarises the BASE-ASIA (2006) and 7-SEAS/Dongsha (2010) spring campaigns in northern Southeast Asia and a 28-paper special issue characterising biomass-burning aerosols and related pollutants near source and in sink regions.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: The review (written for the 7SEAS programme) describes Southeast Asia as one of the most complex aerosol systems in the world, identifies biomass burning as its most studied aerosol issue, and concludes that satellite aerosol data products diverge greatly owing to known artifacts.
note: Crossref confirms metadata (Atmos Res 122:403-468, 2013). Abstract paraphrase obtained from UMT/Iowa repository page, not the publisher (403).

supports: MODIS hotspot and aerosol-assimilation analysis for the Maritime Continent finds ENSO is the largest factor in burning, enhanced also by El Nino Modoki, while the Madden-Julian Oscillation largely controls when visible burning occurs.
note: Crossref abstract. NOTE: Maritime Continent (Indonesia/Malaysia), not mainland SE Asia.

supports: For 1997-2006 in Southeast Asia, during strong El Nino years fires contribute up to 200 ug/m3 annual-average PM2.5 near fire sources, about 200 additional days per year exceeding the WHO 50 ug/m3 24-h interim target, and an estimated 10,800 (6,800-14,300) person (~2%) annual increase in regional adult cardiovascular mortality.
note: Abstract from Europe PMC; Crossref: online 2012-08-12, print vol 3 issue 2 (Feb 2013) pp 131-136; year set to 2013.

supports: The authors report that Cambodia, Myanmar and Thailand showed a similar result with less than a 25% increase in hotspot severity from normal to El Nino, positive IOD, or El Nino-positive IOD years, compared with more than 72% (Kalimantan) and 89% (South Sumatra) increases during the strong 2015 El Nino.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract; mainland-SEA ENSO modulation is weaker than in maritime SEA.

supports: GEOS-Chem for March and September 2014 underestimates regional aerosol burden relative to satellite AOD (20-52%) and ground PM (up to 54%), especially in early burning season (March); sensitivity modifications improve March agreement to within 31%.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Useful as model-underestimation evidence for SE Asia biomass-burning PM (a model, not CAMS specifically).

supports: Title states it examines the influence of the zero-burning policy and climate phenomena on ambient PM2.5 patterns and PAH inhalation cancer risk during smoke-haze episodes in Northern Thailand.
note: Metadata verified in Crossref (Atmos Environ 232:117485, 2020) but abstract NOT read (no abstract in Crossref/OpenAlex/PubMed; publisher blocked). Secondhand search snippet suggested lengthening of the haze season under the zero-burning policy - NOT verified, do not cite numbers.

supports: Describes the MODIS Collection 6 active-fire algorithm; MOD14 Collection 6 daytime global commission error was 1.2% versus 2.4% in Collection 5, with reduced omission errors over large fires and reduced false-alarm rates in tropical ecosystems.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: The VIIRS 375 m active-fire algorithm showed small, variable commission errors (<1.2%) for nominal-confidence fire pixels and detected 3x (day) and 25x (night) more fire pixels than the VIIRS 750 m baseline product.
note: Abstract read from the NASA-hosted author PDF (directreadout.sci.gsfc.nasa.gov); metadata from Crossref.

supports: Describes FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), a NASA-funded system that delivers MODIS active-fire data via Internet mapping services and customised e-mail alerts to users in more than 90 countries.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Covers MODIS-era FIRMS (2009), not the current VIIRS/LANCE FIRMS.

supports: Describes AERONET as a NASA-initiated remote-sensing aerosol monitoring network with open-access database, centralized processing, near-real-time processing, and discusses radiometer precision/accuracy and database access.
note: Crossref metadata confirmed; abstract paraphrased from search-result summaries of institutional repository records (mdsoar.org), publisher abstract not retrieved.

supports: AERONET Version 3 provides fully automatic cloud screening and instrument-anomaly quality control for near-real-time and reprocessed data (database reprocessed in 2018), with Level 2.0 AOD available within a month of post-field calibration.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract (truncated read; do not quote uncertainty numbers without re-reading).

supports: The Angstrom exponent is often used as a qualitative indicator of aerosol particle size, with values greater than 2 indicating small particles associated with combustion byproducts and values less than 1 indicating large particles such as sea salt and dust.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: Original source of the wavelength power-law (Angstrom exponent) description of atmospheric extinction by dust; only the bibliographic record (Geografiska Annaler 11(2):156-166) was verified, no abstract exists.
note: Crossref confirms title/year/volume/pages (Taylor & Francis DOI; JSTOR DOI 10.2307/519399 also exists). Content claim not verified beyond title.

supports: The CAMS reanalysis (ECMWF; 2003-2016 at the time, ~80 km resolution) assimilates satellite CO, NO2, AOD and ozone retrievals and has smaller biases than the previous MACC and CAMS-interim reanalyses against independent ozone, CO, NO2 and AOD observations.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Abstract does NOT evaluate surface PM2.5.

supports: Describes the evolution of NOAA's HYSPLIT trajectory and dispersion modelling system over 30 years and highlights applications including smoke from wild fires.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: CAMS global atmospheric composition forecast (cycle 46r1) PM2.5 evaluated against hourly Malaysian observations 2018-2020 performed generally weaker (CSI = 31%, R2 = 0.36) than reported elsewhere (CSI = 20-54%, R2 = 0.32-0.79), missed local spatiotemporal variation but better captured the regional 2019 transboundary haze episode; authors recommend bias-correction.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. No signed bias number in abstract; skill metrics only.

supports: CAMS PM2.5 forecasts for 2017-2018 in China showed mean correlation 0.31-0.45 and RMSE 38-83 ug/m3 (US: 0.24-0.42; 8.30-16.76 ug/m3) as lead time grew from 3 h to 120 h, with large spatially varied modelling biases; a random-forest bias correction substantially reduced them.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. China/US, not SE Asia.

supports: Against 1,675 Chinese monitoring stations (2014-2020), CAMS significantly OVERestimates PM2.5 and PM10 over most regions (especially urban and desert areas), and both CAMS and MERRA-2 substantially underestimate the lowest concentrations over the Tibetan Plateau and Qinghai.
note: Crossref confirms metadata; abstract quoted from KNMI publication page. IMPORTANT: this contradicts a presumed 'CAMS underestimates PM2.5 in Asia' narrative; do not cite as underestimation.

title: Theorie der horizontalen Sichtweite
container: Beitraege zur Physik der freien Atmosphaere
supports: Original theory of horizontal visibility (Part I) underlying the visibility-extinction (Koschmieder) relation; only the bibliographic record was verified, no abstract exists.
note: Verified via Met Office National Meteorological Library record (reprint in 'Selected Papers on Scattering in the Atmosphere', 1989): 'Reprinted from Beitraege zur Physik der freien Atmosphaere, Vol. XII, 1924. Part I: pp. 33-53.' Part II ('Kontrast und Sichtweite') exists; its pages not verified. No DOI. Content of the law itself is not quoted from the 1924 text.

supports: For 2016-2018 China, the Spearman correlation between PM2.5 and visibility-derived surface extinction coefficient was significant at most stations (national median rho = 0.67 in winter), with lower rho (<0.4) in the cleanest regions, partly attributed to the ~30 km maximum visibility threshold.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract; a modern link between visibility/extinction and PM2.5 (China). Also uses Spearman correlation.

supports: Proposes the dark channel prior, based on the observation that most local patches in outdoor haze-free images contain some pixels with very low intensity in at least one colour channel, enabling estimation of haze thickness and a depth map from a single image.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. TPAMI 33(12):2341-2353 (2011; online 2010).

supports: Six image features extracted from outdoor images of Beijing, Shanghai and Phoenix, combined with sun position, date, time, geographic and weather data, were used to predict PM2.5 index, and the abstract reports 'good prediction' with different features of different significance (no numeric accuracy in abstract).
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Numbers (R, RMSE) must be read in the full text if wanted.

supports: Extinction coefficient computed from commercial-camera RGB pixels correlated with PM2.5 mass concentration at R2 = 0.7 (higher than with visibility data), despite a limited mass range; derived mass extinction efficiency was (10.8 +/- 6.9) m2/g, higher than earlier Northeast Asia values, which the authors flag as needing further long-term study.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract; limitations as stated in abstract (limited mass range; extinction efficiency varies with aerosol size/composition).

supports: Hourly sky/building photographs from a high-rise in Bangkok with nearest-station ground truth: a hybrid CNN-LSTM model outperformed conventional CNN models by 5% (estimation) and 30% (forecasting).
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract; Thai study. Abstract gives only relative improvements, not R2/RMSE.

supports: A VGG16-LSTM model integrating surveillance images with numerical data forecast PM2.5 and PM10 for 2021 Shanghai with R2 0.9459/0.9045 and RMSE 4.79/11.51 ug/m3; transfer to two Kaohsiung stations gave average R2 0.9728/0.9365 for PM2.5/PM10; the authors list expanding datasets and optimising architectures as future work.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. NOTE the images are integrated with multi-source numerical (atmospheric/meteorological) data, so skill is not image-only.

supports: Low-cost PM sensors are subject to biases and calibration dependencies (meteorology, sensor age, aerosol source, composition, refractive index), corrected with methods from linear/quadratic models to machine learning, and the review sets out best practices for obtaining high-quality data.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: More than 1500 low-cost sensors are installed in Thailand; co-located with an FEM reference at Chiang Mai (north), Bangkok and Ubon Ratchathani, PMS7003 performance was acceptable in Chiang Mai (dry season) and Ubon Ratchathani after multiple-regression calibration (slope 0.829-0.945, R2 0.880-0.934, RMSE 4.3-5.1 ug/m3), while errors were mainly at low concentrations and high humidity and sensors underestimated in congested Bangkok.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: In Chiang Mai (April-May 2018, 25 districts with DustBoy devices), trained health staff's human-sighted visual range reached 79.21% accuracy for PM10 but only 26.49% for PM2.5 (classified 'not useful'), and was ineffective at twilight, on rainy/cloudy days or with humidity >65%.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract (International Journal of Public Health Asia Pacific, 2024). Mentions DustBoy devices as the reference instruments. Small journal; check Crossref JSON for volume/issue.

supports: Original paper introducing Model Output Statistics (MOS) for objective weather forecasting (J. Appl. Meteor. 11(8):1203-1211); only bibliographic record checked (no abstract in Crossref).
note: Crossref confirms title/authors/journal/volume/issue/pages/year.

title: Forecast Verification: A Practitioner's Guide in Atmospheric Science
supports: Standard reference text on forecast verification methods in atmospheric science (edited volume, 2nd edition; ISBN 978-0-470-66071-3 hardcover, 978-1-119-96107-9 e-book).
note: Wiley product page: hardcover Dec 2011, e-book Jan 2012, O-book Feb 2012 (cite as 2012 or 2011 per Wiley hardcover date); Crossref DOI 10.1002/9781119960003 lists editors Jolliffe & Stephenson. It is an EDITED volume (chapters by several authors), not authored by the two.

title: Statistical Methods in the Atmospheric Sciences
supports: Standard textbook on statistical methods in the atmospheric sciences (4th edition, 2019).
note: Crossref book DOI lists ISBN 9780128158234, publisher Elsevier; Elsevier shop page shows 4th edition (9 June 2019). 'Academic Press' imprint NOT confirmed on the pages read. A 5th edition (ISBN 978-0-443-49002-6, 2026) exists per Crossref chapter DOIs - decide which edition to cite.

supports: Origin of the Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion (JASA 22(158):209-212); only bibliographic record checked.
note: Crossref confirms.

supports: Original bootstrap paper (Annals of Statistics 7(1):1-26); only bibliographic record checked.
note: Crossref confirms.

supports: Original source of the rank correlation coefficient (Am. J. Psychol. 15(1)); only the bibliographic record was checked.
note: Crossref gives start page 72 only; end page 101 is from standard citation (not read from Crossref) - confirm before typesetting.

supports: Statistical Science 16(2):101-133 review of interval estimation for a binomial proportion (optional extra for Wilson interval justification); only bibliographic record checked.
note: Crossref confirms; not requested - optional.

authors: Chiang Mai University Climate Change Data Center (CCDC)
title: CMU CCDC website - DustBoy PM2.5 network pages (status, API, installation guide)
supports: The CCDC site hosts DustBoy menus (What is DustBoy, DustBoy status, DustBoy API, installation guide, sensor performance and USEPA calibration reports) and PM2.5 data pages.
note: Page text does not itself state the operator relationship to Chiang Mai University, number of stations, or sensor model; the Theerawasttanasiri 2024 paper reports DustBoy devices installed in Chiang Mai districts, and Dejchanchaiwong 2023 reports >1500 low-cost sensors in Thailand (not specific to DustBoy). Do not state a DustBoy station count without a source.

supports: Using administrative cycling data from Sydney, an air quality alert reduces cycling by 14-35% (a substantial behavioural response), robust across specifications, and the authors also find evidence of 'alert fatigue'.
note: Crossref confirms metadata (Resour. Energy Econ. 49:165-185, 2017). Abstract paraphrase/short quote taken from EconPapers page (publisher abstract not retrieved).

supports: With English local-authority panel data, there is evidence of avoidance behaviour in response to air pollution warnings for children's asthma admissions (where avoidance is less costly), but ignoring avoidance does not produce a statistically significant underestimate of the health effect of air pollution.
note: Abstract from Europe PMC.

supports: Cochrane review found conflicting evidence on health-care usage from three studies of air pollution alerts (one non-randomised trial of 35 participants reporting increased emergency attendances; two randomised trials of 1553 participants reporting little to no difference), rated very uncertain, and inconsistent effects of alerts and education on adherence; the authors conclude lack of evidence limits conclusions.
note: Abstract from Europe PMC (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021). Important counter-evidence: alert effectiveness on health outcomes is unproven.

supports: A systematic review of 37 studies of air-pollution communication campaigns found avoidance behaviour (e.g. reducing outdoor activity) was most commonly studied, that actionable, targeted localized information and positive framing are likely to help, and that smartphones enable targeted engagement but care is needed not to transfer responsibility from authorities to individuals.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: Reviews citizen-science air-quality monitoring initiatives in Asia, Africa, Europe and Latin America and finds little research on how citizen-generated data feed evidence-based policymaking; proposes a methodology combining scientific evidence, participation and deliberation.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: A literature review of low-cost sensing found no clear answer on fitness for purpose (lack of manufacturer performance specifications and agreed minimum targets), and that about 30% of 17 large applied projects were commercial and/or crowd-funded, signalling a paradigm change from monitoring led by government organisations.
note: Abstract from Europe PMC.

supports: Evaluating 24 identical units of a commercial low-cost sensor platform against CEN reference analysers showed performance varies by unit, time and conditions; such platforms present low accuracy for regulatory or health purposes but can provide relative and aggregated information on air quality (e.g. awareness raising).
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

authors: Hydro-Informatics Institute (HII) [host domain hii.or.th]; project funded via National Research Council of Thailand and Kasetsart University grant
title: Tam Roy Pao (ตามรอยเผา) - open burning / burn-scar monitoring system
supports: The site (Thai) states the system was developed under the project 'research and development of a system to process, report and monitor open burning areas using high-resolution satellite imagery', funded by a National Research Council of Thailand and Kasetsart University research-promotion grant for B.E. 2567 (2024), and provides a dashboard for 8 northern provinces, a web map, monthly/seasonal burn-scar downloads (CSV, GeoTIFF, TMS, API), 7-day 20 m burn-scar products (77 Sentinel-2 grid tiles) and agricultural burn areas split by rice, sugarcane, maize and mixed crops.
note: Page read directly (HTML fetched). Developer attribution to HII is inferred from the hii.or.th domain; the page text I read names the NRCT and Kasetsart University grant but I did not find an explicit 'developed by HII' line. No peer-reviewed paper for Tam Roy Pao found. Related peer-reviewed Thai burned-area work: suwanprasit2024obia.

supports: Sentinel-2A (10 m) with object-based image analysis mapped burned areas in five Chiang Mai districts from a 27 Feb 2018 image and was 85.2% accurate against 500 random burned points from an existing burned-area dataset.
note: Crossref + Europe PMC abstract. Not the Tam Roy Pao paper; a related peer-reviewed example.

authors: Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA)
title: Disaster Platform - Fire (hotspot service)
supports: GISTDA's Disaster Platform (page title 'Fire | Disaster Platform', described as a decision-support system for disaster management) offers a fire view with province/district/sub-district selectors alongside flood and drought views.
note: Page fetched; content is a JS map app. News reports (Nation, Pattaya Mail 2026) say GISTDA hotspot counts come from Suomi NPP VIIRS - secondary sources, not read at GISTDA. Older URLs (firms.gistda.or.th) not confirmed.

title: Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS)
supports: NASA LANCE FIRMS web portal exists and distributes active-fire data (page title 'NASA | LANCE | FIRMS'); detailed dataset claims not extracted.
note: Only the page title was confirmed by fetch; read the FIRMS 'About' page before stating latency/resolution claims.

title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (signed Kuala Lumpur, 10 June 2002; in force 25 November 2003)
supports: Official text of the Agreement: Article 3(1) recognises the Parties' sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental and developmental policies and the responsibility to ensure activities within their jurisdiction do not harm other States; Article 29 provides entry into force on the sixtieth day after deposit of the sixth instrument; done at Kuala Lumpur on the tenth day of June 2002.
note: Text read from the ASEAN agreement-repository PDF (pdftotext). Signing date/place confirmed also by the ASEAN Haze Portal and ASEAN Environment Knowledge Hub.

title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (status and ratification table)
supports: The official ASEAN Haze Portal table (as of 20 January 2015) gives date of ratification/approval and date of deposit: Thailand 10 September 2003 / 26 September 2003; Indonesia 14 October 2014 / 20 January 2015; Myanmar 5 March 2003 / 17 March 2003 (also Brunei 27 Feb/23 Apr 2003; Cambodia 24 Apr/9 Nov 2006; Lao PDR 19 Dec 2004/13 Jul 2005; Malaysia 3 Dec 2002/18 Feb 2003; Philippines 1 Feb/4 Mar 2010; Singapore 13/14 Jan 2003; Viet Nam 24 Mar/29 May 2003); signed 10 June 2002 in Kuala Lumpur; ratified by all ASEAN Member States; ASEAN Secretariat serves as Interim ACC.
note: Live site (hazeportal.asean.org / haze.asean.org) is behind a JS bot-gate or unreachable; read via Internet Archive copy of the official page. Derived check: the sixth deposit was Thailand's (26 Sep 2003) -> +60 days = 25 Nov 2003, consistent with Art. 29 and the stated entry-into-force date.

title: Indonesia Deposits Instrument of Ratification of the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution
container: ASEAN Environment Knowledge Hub (media release, 21 January 2015; Internet Archive copy)
supports: On 20 January 2015 Indonesia deposited its instrument of ratification with the ASEAN Secretary-General (approved by Indonesia's Parliament through Law No. 26 Year 2014); the Agreement was signed on 10 June 2002 in Kuala Lumpur and entered into force on 25 November 2003.
note: Official ASEAN media release, read via Internet Archive.

title: Roadmap on ASEAN Cooperation towards Transboundary Haze Pollution Control with Means of Implementation (2016-2020) (Haze-free Roadmap)
supports: The first Haze-free Roadmap (2016-2020) was adopted at COP-12 on 11 August 2016 in Kuala Lumpur, with a vision of a Transboundary Haze-free ASEAN by 2020 and indicators including more days with good/moderate air quality, fewer hotspots below Alert Level 2, and a smaller transboundary haze area.
note: Read via Internet Archive copy of the official page.

title: Media Release: 17th ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on the Environment and 18th Meeting of the COP to the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (Vientiane, 23 August 2023)
supports: The Meetings welcomed the adoption of the Second Roadmap on ASEAN Cooperation towards Transboundary Haze Pollution Control with Means of Implementation (Haze-free Roadmap) 2023-2030 and the Second ASEAN Peatland Management Strategy 2023-2030, endorsed the ASEAN Investment Framework for Haze-free Sustainable Land Management, and noted ASMC's assessment that Alert Level 3 was issued for the Mekong sub-region on 2 March 2023 and that Mekong-region hotspot count was ~57% higher in 2023 than 2022 over January-August.
note: PDF read in full. NOTE the instrument is called the 'Second Roadmap ... 2023-2030', not an 'ASEAN Cooperation Plan 2023-2030'. A dedicated ASEAN document page (asean.org/book/the-second-roadmap...) is behind a bot-gate; the document text itself was not read.

title: ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC)
supports: ASMC was established in January 1993, is hosted by Meteorological Service Singapore (NEA), and is the designated body to monitor and assess land and forest fires and transboundary smoke haze affecting ASEAN, providing monthly weather and haze outlooks, satellite images, hotspot information, air quality information and fire danger rating.
note: Read via Internet Archive copy of the official page.

title: The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution: Prospects for Compliance and Effectiveness in Post-Suharto Indonesia
supports: The article (by Alan Khee-Jin Tan) examines the prospects for compliance with and effectiveness of the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in post-Suharto Indonesia; only the bibliographic listing was verified (no abstract read).
note: Title, author, journal, volume 13 and issue 3 confirmed on the NYU Environmental Law Journal volume-13 contents page. Year 2005 and pages 647-722 come from search-result snippets of the author's NUS CV (could not open the CV; other sources give differing end pages) - CONFIRM pages in HeinOnline/Westlaw before typesetting. No DOI.

supports: Argues that Indonesia's January 2015 ratification will not be an immediate game changer because the agreement's mechanisms are too weak; it is designed according to the ASEAN way, a non-binding approach based on state sovereignty and non-intervention.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: Content analysis of 2,231 newspaper articles from Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia on the 1997, 2005 and 2013 haze crises shows coverage shifting from health/economic impacts toward blaming Indonesia for not ratifying the 2002 ASEAN agreement, and criticism of palm-oil investors and of ASEAN itself.
note: Crossref confirms metadata; abstract read as a paraphrase from LSE Research Online (researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/56043).

supports: World Development 30(3):429-441 'Transboundary pollution in Southeast Asia: The Indonesian fires' - indexed abstract text (via ASEAN Haze Portal/ADINET records) describes a transboundary haze problem with severe economic ramifications and proposes stakeholder-based cost sharing; abstract itself not read from publisher.
note: Crossref confirms bibliographic details. NOTE the user-supplied title 'Transboundary haze' differs: the actual title is 'Transboundary Pollution in Southeast Asia: The Indonesian Fires'.

supports: Contemporary Southeast Asia 37(2):183-210 examines the influence of international law upon ASEAN approaches to transboundary haze pollution; abstract not available in Crossref/OpenAlex (only issue line).
note: Crossref confirms authors Nurhidayah, Alam, Lipman (+ possibly others) and pages; content claim limited to title.

supports: Indonesia's lawmakers unanimously ratified the AATHP on 16 September 2014; eight of ten member states had ratified by 2006 and nine by 2010; the negotiated AATHP was 'soft' and thus low-cost for domestic stakeholders, yet key domestic actors had little appetite to ratify and neighbours' pressure was limited until the 2010s.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Note date nuance: parliament 16 Sep 2014 vs ASEAN-portal table 14 Oct 2014 (ratification/approval) and 20 Jan 2015 (deposit).

title: The Haze Problem in Southeast Asia: Palm Oil and Patronage

title: Challenges in tackling PM2.5 crisis (TDRI Insight; first published in the Bangkok Post, 12 April 2023)
supports: TDRI argues the haze problem is 'a deep-seated structural problem' of 'inert bureaucracy and silo culture', that the panel overseeing the PM2.5 crisis 'operates as an ad hoc body without any consistency', that agencies bargain with the Budget Bureau for their share, that provincial governors face rules barring them from taking budget from other departments, and that local agencies 'don't get a budget for PM2.5' (provincial budget fell from 48.6 billion baht in 2018 to 19.6 billion baht in 2020).

title: Management and Reduction of Burning Practice in Agricultural Areas and Policy Recommendations to Tackle PM2.5 in Thailand (1st revised and updated edition, January 2022)
container: Thailand Environment Institute Foundation; supported by Pure Earth, PCD (MoNRE), GAHP, UNEP, APCAP
supports: The report states the Cabinet made particulate matter a National Agenda on 12 February 2019 and adopted the Action Plan to Drive the National Agenda on 1 October 2019 (via MoNRE, endorsed by the National Environment Board), assigns measures to several bodies (Ministries of Agriculture and Cooperatives, Finance, Industry and Energy, and the Bangkok Metropolitan Authority and provincial administrations) and lists a sub-committee on forest fire, smog and particulate pollution under the National Committee on Disaster Prevention and Relief.
note: PDF read (pdftotext). It does not give a clean agency-by-agency mandate table for DDPM, DNP, GISTDA, HII or RFD; and it is a policy-institute report supported by PCD/UNEP.

supports: In a quantitative assessment of burning restrictions in Thailand's PM2.5 control plan, institutional/social barriers delay implementation more than technical/economic barriers, leaving about twice the PM2.5 emissions of an effectively implemented policy over 10-20 years; overcoming them costs about US$14 million a year (~70% of the US$21 million planned for burning control in 2026).
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract.

supports: Analysis of three Thai national newspapers over 25 years plus fieldwork shows the Chiang Mai 'haze crisis' narrative developed through debates over forest use, agro-capitalism and legitimate political power (a framing/politics paper, not an agency-mandate analysis).
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Context for governance framing.

supports: Ethnographic work 2019-2024 argues that official data only partially support claims of worsening northern Thai haze, and that solutions are framed as technocratic challenges rather than restructuring of socioeconomic relations of production.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. Relevant caveat for a monitoring-to-warning system paper.

title: Notification of the National Environment Board: Setting the standard of particulate matter not exceeding 2.5 microns in ambient air (signed 23 June 2022; Royal Gazette Vol. 139, Special Part 163 Ng, 8 July 2022, p. 21-22)
container: Royal Gazette (copy hosted by Pollution Control Department, pcd.go.th)
supports: The notification (Thai) repeals NEB Notification No. 36 (B.E. 2553) and sets the 24-hour PM2.5 standard at not more than 50 ug/m3 through 31 May 2023 and not more than 37.5 ug/m3 from 1 June 2023 onward, and an annual arithmetic mean of not more than 15 ug/m3; in force from the day after publication (9 July 2022); monitoring by FRM/FEM-equivalent methods including light scattering.
note: Read directly (PDF text of the gazette pages). CORRECTION to the brief: the 37.5 ug/m3 24-h standard took effect 1 June 2023, NOT 1 January 2023. PCD's own news item also states the standard 'in force from 1 June 2566 (2023)'. The Royal Gazette site itself returned 403 to curl, so the PCD-hosted copy of the gazette pages was used; Greenpeace Thailand's page wrongly says annual 25 ug/m3 (the gazette text says 15).

title: Notification of the Pollution Control Department: Air Quality Index of Thailand B.E. 2566 (2023) (dated 16 May 2023; Royal Gazette Vol. 140, Special Part 157 Ng, 3 July 2023)
supports: Thai AQI 2023 has five levels (0-25 very good, 26-50 good, 51-100 moderate, 101-200 beginning to affect health, 201+ affects health) with 24-h PM2.5 breakpoints 0-15.0, 15.1-25.0, 25.1-37.5, 37.6-75.0 and 75.1+ ug/m3 (PM10 24-h: 0-50, 51-80, 81-120, 121-180, 181+); AQI 100 equals the ambient standard; it repeals the PCD AQI notification of 24 September 2018.

title: Air quality in Thailand: Understanding the regulatory context (SEI working paper)
supports: The SEI desk review states that 'many disparate Ministries and agencies are involved with different mandates', that policies are owned and enforced by the agency under which the source falls with 'little integration across sectors', that local and provincial governments 'frequently lack the necessary data and mandate to take enforcement action', and that there is 'no overarching agency with a responsibility for clean air'; its policy table also records provincial authority (Public Disaster Prevention and Mitigation Act 2007) to prohibit burning for 60 days.
note: PDF read (pdftotext), February 2021; short quotes taken from pages 18-24. Author list from the title page (Jaee Nikam, Diane Archer, Chirat Nopsert; editor Molly Killeen). Independent non-profit research institute.

supports: For 15 March-15 April 2019 over northern Thailand (observed PM2.5 40-240 ug/m3), WRF-Chem with GOCART and MOSAIC aerosol schemes captured spatiotemporal variation but underestimated observed PM2.5 magnitudes by about 24% and 27%, respectively; EDGAR-HTAP anthropogenic emissions gave more realistic results than CAMS-GLOB-ANT in most regions.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. NOTE: this is a regional chemistry model (WRF-Chem), not the CAMS reanalysis/forecast; only the CAMS-GLOB-ANT emission inventory is CAMS-related. Do not describe it as CAMS PM2.5 bias.

supports: CAMS reanalysis evaluated for 2016-2023 over the Himawari-8 area (China, Indonesia, Australia): CAMS captures large-scale pollution episodes but discrepancies in ground-level concentrations are apparent, especially during short-term events with vertical aerosol stratification.
note: Crossref + OpenAlex abstract. No bias numbers or sign in the abstract.
